newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan markets hurt by spillover from US sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Japan markets hurt by spillover from US sell-off.

text.p: Taking their cue from a sell-off on U.S. markets, Japanese stocks sagged on Thursday and the dollar and bonds were buffeted by lingering jitters about interest rates and the allure of U.S. assets.

But the blow was softer than many had expected, and Tokyo prices recovered some ground in afternoon trade as dealers grew wary of selling too aggressively before seeing whether U.S. markets can bounce back on Thursday.

Tokyo stocks took an early battering along with most other Asian bourses after a sharp drop on Wall Street overnight, where fears of rising U.S. interest rates helped knock around one percent off the value of the Dow.
But Japanese shares clawed back by the close to post a modest drop of only a third of a percent, with the benchmark Nikkei 225 average finishing at 20,501.20, down 67.18 points.

"The market wants to see how the U.S. markets recover later today and how the settlement goes tomorrow," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities, referring to future and options settlement for December due on Friday.
On the currency market, the dollar struggled to shake off Wednesday's fears that U.S. assets such as Treasuries may be losing their appeal and U.S. interest rates may rise.

By late trading the greenback was mixed against major currencies, standing at 112.89 yen and 1.5410 marks compared with its late U.S. level of around 112.97 yen and 1.5378 marks, after coming off its lows.
"Short-covering against the yen helped the dollar pick itself up today, and there don't seem to be that many long positions accumulated in the market," said a dealer at a trust bank.

Although bargain-hunting helped lift U.S. Treasuries during Tokyo trading, Japanese government bonds put in a weak performance, hurt by the possibility that Japan's rockbottom interest rates may rise sooner than expected.

A Bank of Japan official was quoted in a financial daily as saying the central bank may adjust its easy monetary policy before assessing the possible economic impact of a consumption tax hike due next April.
Japan's key interest rate has been held at a record low of 0.5 percent for more than a year to bolster the nation's fragile economic recovery.

Wednesday's anxiety attack on U.S. markets was fuelled by comments from a senior Goldman Sachs official who questioned whether Japanese investors were losing their appetite for U.S. Treasuries. Such a trend could put upward pressure on U.S. interest rates and hurt U.S. stocks, threatening a major correction to Wall Street's record-breaking run.
In a sign of the nervousness on Wall Street, Wednesday's steep descent was speeded by a host of unsubstantiated rumours about corporate earnings.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury fell more than 1-3/4 points in U.S. trading on Wednesday, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, shot up to 6.63 percent -- its highest since early November -- against 6.49 percent on Tuesday.
